articles.title: Opinion - Democrats win an election and immediately move to subvert democracy
articles.summary: The standard for impeachment is not "kind of legalizing a lot."
articles.body:
It appears democracy is too important to be left to voters.

After Democrats ran on "saving democracy" from its imminent destruction, many voters may be a bit confused by the actions of their newly elected representatives. Democratic politicians and pundits are moving to negate certain results in the last election and to circumvent future votes on key reforms. The country could soon be experiencing the greatest changes to our constitutional system in 250 years, but the public will have little to say about it.

In Seattle, socialist Mayor Katie Wilson announced that she and the city would move to block a statewide initiative approved by 36 of 39 counties. The public voted to require the separation of boys and girls in K-12 sports. It is an issue that has overwhelming support among both Democrats and Republicans, with polls showing roughly 70 percent of Americans supporting girls' sports for girls alone.

But Wilson and others do not like the decision, so they are seeking to protect the public from their supposedly bad choices.

In Colorado, Governor-elect Phil Weiser (D), the former dean at the University of Colorado Law School, was a prominent figure in the "No Kings" protests before the election. But after his election, he decided that the voters' democratic decisions on transgender policies were inherently flawed and he would have to correct them.

Colorado voters passed a ban on male athletes in girls and women's sports. Proposition 134 defined girls as having female reproductive organs and boys as having male reproductive organs. So that there would be no ambiguity later, the drafters expressly added that "students assigned male at birth play only on boys teams or co-ed teams and vice versa for females."

The public also passed Proposition 135, banning gender-affirming surgeries for minors.

Weiser, however, declared that, with a new supermajority in both houses, Democrats would "have to take a look at these anti-trans measures ... to fix [them] and provide a much more human and sound approach."

This is the same politician who recently insisted that he was "defending democracy" and standing for "our government of the people, by the people, and for the people." But apparently, the last thing large-D Democrats want to do is actually listen to the people.

The "saving democracy" crowd seems to have a very serious problem with democracy.

In Alaska, the champions of democracy who supported Alaska Democratic Senatorial nominee Mary Peltola (D) worked to put a decoy "Dan Sullivan" on the ballot with the sole aim of confusing voters. The New York Times reported in painful detain that the effort had been coordinated at the highest level of the Democratic establishment, including the involvement of the law group of Marc Elias, the notorious lawyer involved in the Steele Dossier controversy .

In the prior election, many of these same figures supported efforts to prevent voters from voting for Trump and other Republicans — requiring the Supreme Court to step in and restore to the ballot the candidate who went on to win the popular vote.

Democrats are now planning to fundamentally change the constitutional system. As one Harvard law professor explained it, these committed democracy-defenders will guarantee that Republicans "never win another election." The key is to prevent voters from actually voting on any of the changes.

Democratic leaders are openly talking about packing the Supreme Court to allow an array of changes by judicial fiat. Although many Americans still oppose court packing, this could technically be done by a vote of Congress.

There is also a building effort to effectively abolish the Electoral College , to increase the power of high-population blue states without actually seeking a constitutional amendment. Securing the White House after negating the Electoral College would mean that many of these changes could be accomplished by a simple majority vote.

There is also an effort to simply declare the District of Columbia a state, without a constitutional amendment to alter the status of D.C. as a federal enclave and non-state in Article I, Section 8. (Democrats are also seeking to add Puerto Rico, to give Democrats an even greater edge in the Senate.) Past polls show considerable opposition to making a state out of the federal district whose current boundaries were carved out of Maryland's territory.

The key is to make these changes through Washington rather than giving citizens a vote on such fundamental changes. A packed court alone would bring radical changes, particularly with Democrats pointing to far-left Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson as their model for the new stacked court.

This has long been a pattern for far-left political movements. In my book " Rage and the Republic ," I discuss how the French radicals called the Jacobins took power by marshaling the rage of the people, but then ruled the nation as a small elite. While espousing faith in the "general will" of the people, the Jacobins concentrated power in the hands of brutal committees with such blood-soaked figures as Maximilien Robespierre.

The Jacobins used the language of popular government to assume power, but not to share it with the people. While we have a representative democracy, the Framers still wanted citizens to approve major changes to our system. Today the new Jacobins are seeking structural changes to guarantee their own power while offering the voters ways to vent their rage rather than play a role in governance.

Taking another page from the Jacobins, Democratic leaders are promising heads. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) promised "many, many, many investigations" into what she calls the "criminals" of the opposing party. She even recently suggested that conservative Supreme Court justices might be impeached for ruling against the wishes of her party.

"I mean, of course, this Supreme Court as well has also kind of legalized a lot of his criminality," she said. Of course, the standard for impeachment is not "kind of legalizing a lot." But that is just the standard in the Constitution, which is itself becoming increasingly irrelevant to the Democratic Party's agenda.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of " Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution ."

articles.title: Dems' California redistricting mastermind flips script after helping party win 5 GOP seats: 'Kill'
articles.summary: Paul Mitchell, architect of California's Prop 50, claims Democrats should establish national standards to end partisan gerrymandering for good.
articles.body: The architect of California's Democratic-friendly redistricting plan, which helped the party flip five Republican-held House seats in November's midterm elections, is now calling on Democrats to put an end to partisan gerrymandering nationwide. Paul Mitchell claimed in a San Francisco Chronicle op-ed published Wednesday that lawmakers should "kill partisan gerrymandering for good." His comments come after California voters approved Proposition 50 in November 2025, temporarily replacing the state's independently drawn congressional districts with a Democratic-friendly map for elections through 2030. Mitchell acknowledged in his op-ed that Proposition 50 was designed to benefit Democrats, but defended it as a temporary response to Republican-led redistricting efforts before calling for an end to partisan mapmaking altogether. "I wasn’t trying to do this [op-ed] to time with anyone’s efforts to do further gerrymandering," Mitchell told Fox News Digital on Thursday evening. "I always planned on doing this as soon as the election was over, and I even did a CNN interview with Elex Michaelson during the election coverage where I said that the answer needs to be to stop this redistricting war and actually fix the problem." REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES Mitchell went on to say that Prop 50 was "the right response" to Texas Republicans' redistricting push. "Prop 50 was the right response to what Republicans in TX were doing, but recall that when TX started doing this, our approach wasn’t to just start redistricting ourselves, we did a lot of work trying to get TX to not start the redistricting wars," he told Fox News Digital. "If then someone had said "congress will be banning mid-decade redistricting" we would have been all for it. And I supported the legislation by Zoe Lofgren that would have [set up] national redistricting standards." Mitchell argued that Republicans' midterm losses could make them more receptive to redistricting reform after years of opposing it. "What makes now really important is that Republicans, who have opposed redistricting reform, should now realize that they lost in this war, so getting out of future wars is something maybe they would take more seriously now," he told Fox News Digital. As for California, Mitchell believes the Proposition 50 maps will remain in place through 2030 and said the focus should be on restoring a fairer redistricting process in 2031. He called for Congress to prohibit mid-decade redistricting but argued that such a restriction alone would not prevent partisan gerrymandering when states redraw their maps after each census. "I think the best solution would be independent commissions in every state," he said. The California Democratic Party touted Prop 50 as a "direct response to a Republican power grab orchestrated by President [Donald] Trump and state leaders in Texas, who redrew congressional district lines to gain five more seats in the U.S. House of Representatives." Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom similarly claimed in a Nov. 4, 2025 social media post that Prop 50 "is about standing up to bullies like Donald Trump." Mitchell's recent op-ed also claims that gerrymandering can erode voters’ ability "to elect the candidates they prefer." Democrats notably succeeded in flipping all five House seats in California targeted by the party's redistricting push in the November midterm elections, the AP reported Nov. 4. BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES "The incoming Congress should make national redistricting a priority, establishing minimum standards for how all states draw their districts," Mitchell wrote in the opinion piece. Mitchell serves as the vice president of Political Data Inc., a California-based bipartisan voter data firm. He is also the owner of Redistricting Partners, a Sacramento-based data consulting firm. Mitchell, across his career, has conducted more than 100 redistrictings for states, cities, school boards and community college districts, including the State of New York Independent Redistricting Commission, the Los Angeles City Council Redistricting Commission and the Long Beach Independent Redistricting Commission, according to Redistricting Partners' website. When asked about whether California's gerrymandered maps were necessary during a Nov. 8 interview on "California Politics 360," Mitchell said it would have been "a huge mistake" for Democrats to "sit" on their "laurels." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Following Democrats' sweeping victories in November's midterm elections, some states have floated redrawing their congressional maps ahead of the 2028 election cycle, Roll Call reported Nov. 9. Meanwhile, outgoing Republican Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp said Nov. 4 that he would not call a special legislative session to redraw congressional maps or limit the powers of the incoming governor before his term ends in January 2027, WABE reported. articles.title: Ayuso sale en defensa de Feijóo por los idiomas con una camiseta de “J’aime les fruits” en Torrejón de Ardoz
articles.standfirst: La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid también ha cargado contra Pedro Sánchez
articles.summary: La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid también ha cargado contra Pedro Sánchez
articles.body: La presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, ha participado este sábado 14 de noviembre en un mitin del Partido Popular en Torrejón de Ardoz, donde lució una camiseta con el lema en francés “J'aime les fruit” (Me gusta la fruta) y dirigió nuevas críticas al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. El acto se celebró ante unas 900 personas a quince días de las elecciones generales previstas para el 29 de noviembre. "¿Habláis francés? ¿Cómo inglés? ¡Fantástico! Bien. Muy buenos días a todos", comenzó diciendo Ayuso, quien empleó la traducción al francés de su conocida expresión originada en noviembre de 2023 durante el debate de investidura de Sánchez. El gesto buscó defender al candidato del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, de los señalamientos sobre su desconocimiento de inglés. Ayuso censuró la posición internacional del Ejecutivo y afirmó que España quedará fuera del equipo europeo de negociación con Rusia, lo que a su juicio la convierte en “la única gran nación importante de la Unión Europea que no va a pintar absolutamente nada”. En este sentido, la dirigente madrileña arremetió duramente contra el “sanchismo”, al que calificó de “garrapata”, y acusó al ministro Félix Bolaños de pedir “tregua a los jueces” respecto a las investigaciones que afectan al PSOE. Finalmente, apuntó que Sánchez prepara un indulto para el fiscal general del Estado condenado. "Él habla inglés y en su país tenemos a los médicos en huelga desde hace meses. Él habla inglés y en su país ha habido tres accidentes mortales en nueve meses. Él habla inglés y la gente no llega a final de mes. Él habla inglés y ayer en Europa se han juntado todos los países importantes para ir a defender la paz entre Ucrania y Rusia y España no está. ¿De qué nos sirve tu inglés, Pedro?", sentenciaba la presidenta regional, mientras le pedía a Sánchez que se "vaya a su casa a ver series en inglés".

articles.title: Dems descend on Denver to size up 2028. We asked who wants in the race
articles.summary: Josh Shapiro, Elissa Slotkin, Cory Booker and Ruben Gallego tested 2028 messaging at a Denver conference as Chris Van Hollen bowed out early.
articles.body: DENVER — Democrats are already making their case for 2028. Fresh off sweeping midterm victories, party leaders and rising stars descended on Denver for the "What’s Next" conference. Several potential presidential contenders tested their 2028 messaging before a crowd of activists, strategists and operatives. The conversations offered an early look at who may be considering a run and who is already stepping aside. Less than 24 hours after announcing a challenge to longtime Senate Democratic leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., told reporters he was "no longer pursuing" a presidential bid. SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED "I believe that the size and scale of these majorities, provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people," Van Hollen told reporters in Denver, as he pointed what will be at least a 55-seat Democratic majority in the chamber. Van Hollen’s comments came as Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., weighed whether to make another run for the White House in 2028. 'A lot of hard thought' Booker said he is giving "a lot of hard thought" to a potential 2028 presidential campaign, though he said his focus now is pushing for what he called an "American renewal." "My purpose right now, I want to see America in the next five years have the biggest renewal, the biggest resetting of the economic table so it works for all Americans," Booker told Fox News Digital. He pointed to the cost of housing, healthcare and childcare as evidence that many Americans are struggling to get ahead. "The gap I’m concerned about is not the gap between left and right anymore, it’s a gap between the American people and the American dream, and I want to see that gap close," he said. Asked what he might do differently if he ran again after his unsuccessful 2020 campaign, Booker said candidates should be "their authentic self." He also warned that political divisions are pulling the country apart, saying, "We are not each other’s enemies. We are our fellow patriots. And we all need to start pulling in the same direction." 'Won't have any news to make about that any time soon' While Van Hollen ruled out a presidential bid, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic candidate, told reporters in Denver he would not have "any news to make about that anytime soon." Even so, Buttigieg has not ruled out another run. 'We'll let you know' Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, fresh off of major victories in his home state, said, "I've decided to be a loud voice in this process that we're going through right now as a party to put ourselves in the best position to compete." When asked about his 2028 timeline, Shapiro said "that would be a personal decision my wife and my kids and I make." "When we're ready to say something, we'll let you know," he added. 'I haven't made any decisions' Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan told reporters that she was "seriously" considering a 2028 presidential run. "I haven't made any decisions. Whether it's me or somebody else, I just want to be a part of that next generation of leaders going forward that does things differently and understands who they serve," she added. Pointing to a new crop of Democrats elected in the midterms, Slotkin said "we had an amazing election night that elected a whole bunch of new folks who represent that." 'I have to figure out how to still be a good dad and run for office' Meanwhile, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said his young family will be a major consideration in his decision. "I have three kids, nine, three and a one-year-old. You know, it's hard to manage that schedule and I have to figure out how to still be a good dad and run for office," he said. "If I run I'll probably be the only one that has kids that age that doesn't necessarily come from a lot of money. So I'm going to have to figure all that out," he added. THE MISTAKE NEWLY ELECTED DEMS ADMIT THEY CAN’T AFFORD TO MAKE WITH TRUMP AFTER SWEEPING 2026 WINS Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., who has not said whether he will seek the 2028 nomination, used his speech at "What's Next" to argue Democrats can build a winning coalition across the country. "In America, all things are possible," he said, pointing to Democratic victories from New Hampshire to Mississippi. 'We've got a very talented field ... even if I do run' California Rep. Ro Khanna said he is "certainly considering" a 2028 presidential run but has not made a decision. Khanna, one of the few leaders on the progressive left attending a conference organized by a centrist Democratic group, added "I think after the reception here, I'm, more likely to consider it. I mean, but I'm going around the country seeing whether the message will resonate." Asked about his timetable, Khanna told Fox News Digital, "I think starting next year people will be running." "Imagine this, we’ve had three 80-year-old presidents in a row and suddenly you’re going to have a new generation on both sides. I think that’s fantastic for this country," he said. "I'm excited about some of the people if I do run who would be competitors. It’s going to be great. It’s going to showcase America’s talent." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With no clear frontrunner in sight, the Denver conference offered an early look at Democrats testing their messages and weighing whether to seek the party’s nomination.

articles.title: Peltola Nears Alaska Senate Win, Dems Eye 56th Seat
articles.summary: Peltola Nears Alaska Senate Win, Dems Eye 56th Seat
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola has widened her lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's still-undecided U.S. Senate race, moving within striking distance of an outright victory that would give Democrats their 56th Senate seat following sweeping midterm gains.

As of Saturday morning, Peltola had 49.8% of the vote, compared with Sullivan's 46.1%, a margin of more than 10,000 votes.

The Associated Press reported 96% of votes counted, with Peltola receiving 138,240 votes to Sullivan's 127,828.

The former congresswoman gained nearly 2,000 votes on Sullivan in the latest batch of ballots, strengthening her prospects of clearing the 50% threshold needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice voting tabulation.

Peltola's campaign declared victory Friday, insisting the Republican incumbent could no longer overcome her advantage.

"There is no mathematical path for Sullivan to win this race," the campaign said in a statement posted on X.

"When the remaining votes are counted, Mary will decisively be elected as Alaska's next United States Senator," the statement read.

Campaign manager Cheryl Bruce echoed that confidence in a statement to Newsweek.

"As more ballots get counted, it's clear that Mary's victory is all but guaranteed, and Alaskans have resoundingly rejected Dan Sullivan's D.C. self dealing," Bruce said.

"Mary won today's ballot drop by a decisive margin, and remaining votes from Anchorage, Juneau, and rural Alaska will continue to break for Mary, continuing her momentum to the United States Senate.

"Alaskans are ready for a senator who fights to lower costs and takes on D.C. corruption, and when every vote is counted, Mary will deliver for Alaska," Bruce said.

Sullivan's campaign, however, declined to concede.

"We're still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we'll see what happens from there," campaign spokesman Nate Adams told The New York Times on Friday.

The race remained uncalled Saturday, with outstanding ballots potentially determining whether Peltola secures an outright majority or must prevail through ranked-choice voting.

Under Alaska's system, if no candidate receives more than 50% of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidates are eliminated and their supporters' subsequent preferences redistributed until a winner emerges.

Two minor candidates, Republican Gerald Heikes and unaffiliated Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., have collectively captured roughly 4% of the vote.

Democrats recruited both candidates in an effort to weaken the incumbent's support, according to The New York Times.

The Trump administration previously challenged the election over the presence of another candidate named Sullivan, arguing potential voter confusion, but the lawsuit was dismissed.

Alaska has until Nov. 18 to complete its vote count, with ranked-choice tabulation to follow if necessary.

A Peltola victory would represent another significant Democratic pickup in a midterm election that has already delivered the party 55 Senate seats, its largest majority since the early Obama administration.

Peltola, who campaigned on "fish, family, and freedom," would become the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win an Alaska Senate seat in nearly two decades.

Her potential victory would also underscore Republican difficulties in a state President Donald Trump carried by approximately 14 percentage points in 2024, amid voter concerns over high prices, the administration's war in Iran, and tariffs affecting Alaska's economy.

In another major Democratic victory in Alaska, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, has won the state's gubernatorial election, defeating three Republican opponents in a four-way contest, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Kreiss-Tomkins will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, becoming Alaska's youngest governor and the first Democrat elected to the office in more than two decades.

His victory came after national political organizations poured millions into the contest, with Democrats benefiting from a divided Republican field despite Trump's endorsement of Bernadette Wilson.

Meanwhile, Alaska's U.S. House race remains uncalled, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich III leading in a contest expected to proceed to ranked-choice tabulation.

articles.title: A different kind of ticket-splitting
articles.summary: While Democrats won significant victories in recent midterm elections, voters in several states also approved conservative-leaning ballot initiatives regarding school sports and voter identification.
articles.body:
Going into Election Day, we heard a lot about potential ticket splitting in Texas. Maybe Republican Gov. Greg Abbott would win reelection while voters rejected Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Senate race.

But a different kind of ticket splitting may have emerged elsewhere, and it’s worth paying attention to.

Democrats had a wildly good night on Tuesday. Republicans got obliterated. But further down the ballot, voters in some states that flipped to blue approved ballot questions that don’t exactly line up with the Democratic Party platform.

In Washington state, where Republicans haven’t won a governor’s race since 1980, nearly 57 percent of voters supported an initiative to keep males out of girls’ K-12 sports.

In Colorado, voters favored two measures : one requiring sex-based eligibility for school and college athletics and another prohibiting certain gender-related surgeries for minors.

Arizona voters supported restrictions involving school sports, bathrooms, and locker rooms.

We usually think of ticket splitting as voting for a Democrat in one race and a Republican in another. But what about voting for all Democrats while supporting ballot questions that reflect a position more commonly associated with Republicans?

We don’t know how many individual voters did exactly that, but the results suggest something that tends to get lost in all the red-versus-blue election coverage.

Someone can be furious about gas prices, fed up with corruption, frustrated with the direction of the country, or simply repelled by the candidates and still want policies they believe are fair and sensible when it comes to children and schools.

And voting against a Republican doesn’t mean rejecting every position associated with conservatives, any more than voting for a Democrat means embracing every position associated with progressives.

And then there’s the quality of the candidates themselves. Some were deeply flawed, some ran lousy (and lazy!) campaigns, and some seemed to think dissatisfaction with the other party was a substitute for giving voters an actual reason to support them.

That’s what makes the ballot questions so interesting. In some places, voters were rejecting the candidates but supporting their policy positions.

Ballot questions offer something candidate races rarely do: the chance to weigh in on an issue without having to accept everything else that comes with a politician. A vote for governor or senator is a package deal. You’re choosing someone based on a whole collection of issues, priorities, promises, and personal qualities. You might agree with a candidate on five things and still decide the sixth is a dealbreaker. A ballot question strips all of that baggage. It asks voters to make a decision about one policy, without requiring them to sign on to everything else associated with a candidate they can’t stomach.

These ballot question fights are not over. In Washington state and Colorado, opponents are already discussing legal challenges to the measures that voters supported. What happens when the people elected to govern a state disagree with the voters on a specific issue?

And similar ballot questions could be coming to a state near you. A group of citizens recently dropped off signatures in hopes of setting up a women’s sports referendum in Maine, a state where we just saw a six-term Republican incumbent lose her Senate seat.

The blue wave turned out to be a tsunami and that makes these ballot question results even more interesting. If we really want to understand the electorate in these midterms, we need to pay attention to both.

Winning an election and winning an argument are definitely not the same thing.

Erika Sanzi is the senior director of communications for Defending Education.

articles.title: Democrats eye killing Senate filibuster as lawmaker warns move could be a 'double-edged sword'
articles.summary: Ed Markey says the filibuster must be "on the table" as Democrats take the Senate, while Andy Kim warns the move could be a "double-edged sword."
articles.body: Democratic senators are leaving the door open to eliminating the Senate filibuster as their party prepares to take control of the chamber, with one lawmaker saying the move must be on the table while another warned it could be a "double-edged sword." "Obviously, the filibuster is something that has to be on the table," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital when asked about Democrats' plans for the chamber. But Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., warned that changing the rules could carry consequences long after Democrats leave power. SCHUMER, JEFFRIES SIDESTEP QUESTIONS ON NUKING FILIBUSTER, LAUNCHING ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER BLUE WAVE "Some of these things that we see here can be very much a double-edged sword," Kim said. "I'm not saying that's to deter us from doing it if we decide to do it. But I wanna make sure that everyone's clear-eyed about what we're doing." Scrapping the Senate's 60-vote hurdle would allow Democrats to advance most legislation with a simple majority, weakening Republicans' ability to block their agenda — but also giving the GOP the same advantage if it regains control. Fox News Digital pressed the senators on whether Democrats would consider changing the rules while President Donald Trump remains in office or wait until a potential Democratic presidential victory in 2028. "We're discussing a progressive agenda right now and amongst the other Democratic senators," Markey said. "So I'll be listening to everyone's views on what is the best strategy." SCHUMER'S GRIP ON POWER SLIPS AS DEMS BEGIN TO REVOLT AGAINST HIM, EYE NEW LEADERSHIP Trump pressed Senate Republicans to abolish the filibuster when trying to pass the SAVE America Act, warning that Democrats would eliminate it if the party took back the majority — and now they have. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., stayed silent when asked if he would support Democrats getting rid of the filibuster if they win the White House in 2028. Schumer is currently under scrutiny from progressives as the party considers who will lead the Senate after winning back the majority. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced Thursday that he will be running against Schumer for Senate Majority Leader and is in favor of terminating the filibuster, even going as far as characterizing it as "anti-democratic." "My personal view has been all along that the filibuster is an anti-democratic … provision. It's not in our Constitution," Van Hollen said. "It was put in there by senators to enhance their power over the power of the people." SCHUMER FACES MUTINY FROM NEWLY ELECTED SENATE DEMS AS PARTY PREPARES TO SEIZE POWER Kim cautioned that changing Senate rules could set a precedent Democrats might later regret. "When you open the door…you gotta be ready," Kim said. "You don't wanna shoot from the hip when it comes to really big issues that are affecting our country in this way." He suggested pushing legislation "through other means" before jumping to nuking the filibuster. articles.title: Irene Montero, contra Jordi Wild y su pódcast: "Cuatro candidatos y dos verificadores, pero te faltó una feminista para explicarte lo que es la violencia machista"
articles.standfirst: La líder de Podemos no fue invitada al canal del youtuber y no ha dudado en ofrecerse
articles.summary: La líder de Podemos no fue invitada al canal del youtuber y no ha dudado en ofrecerse
articles.body: Las entrevistas realizadas por Jordi Wild en su podcast, ‘The Wild Project’, a tres de los candidatos a la presidencia del Gobierno de cara a las elecciones del 29N (29 de noviembre), está dando mucho de lo que hablar, sobre todo una parte de la charla con Ada Colau, líder del Frente Amplio. En ella, Jordi Wild señala que 44 mujeres asesinadas al año es una cifra muy pequeña y que no representa una alarma social, aunque defiende que es algo contra lo que se debe luchar. Esto no ha gustado a muchos, atacando al creador de contenido diciendo que invisibilizaba a las víctimas. Una de ellas ha sido Irene Montero, líder de Podemos, que le dedicó un vídeo en sus redes sociales ofreciéndose a ir al podcast, ya que no fue invitada como el resto de candidatos: “Jordi Wild ha dicho que 44 mujeres asesinadas en un año no le parece para tanto. Una mujer cada ocho días no es para tanto. No nos matan lo suficiente. Podríamos ser muchas más”, comenzó diciendo. “Todas las mujeres, todos los días, vivimos sabiendo que podríamos ser muchas más y que podemos ser cualquiera. No solo en ser asesinadas, sino en ser controladas, humilladas, insultadas, golpeadas, violadas...”, continuó, añadiendo que esta es solo una forma más de normalizar este tipo de violencia. Pidiéndole, además que use su altavoz para evitar este tipo de cosas: “Utilizas un altavoz tan grande como el que tienes para tratar de menospreciar o ridiculizar la realidad de la violencia machista”. “Porque no todos los hombres, pero siempre hombres, creen que somos objetos de su propiedad, que tienen poder sobre nosotras para decidir lo que nosotras tenemos que hacer con nuestras vidas y para castigarnos si no hacemos lo que ellos creen”, apuntó, llegando a decir que los discursos como el suyo son los que más daño hacen. “Tuviste cuatro candidatos y dos verificadores, pero te faltó una feminista para explicarte lo que es la violencia machista y cómo tienes una responsabilidad muy grande en no volver a ridiculizarla”, sentenció, dejando caer una posible invitación antes de las elecciones.

articles.title: Dems seize on midterm rout to demand ICE reform but polls reveal a twist in who prioritized immigration
articles.summary: Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido and Texas Democrats push 2028 candidates to prioritize immigration reform after flipping Republican-leaning districts.
articles.body: Democrats are seizing on their sweeping midterm victories to demand immigration reform, even as polling shows economic concerns far outpaced it as a priority for both Democratic and Hispanic voters. The push follows Democratic gains nationwide, including wins in Texas congressional districts redrawn to favor Republicans and major upsets in the state’s Senate and gubernatorial races. Some winners are casting the results as a mandate to challenge President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and putting prospective 2028 Democratic presidential candidates on notice. "Whoever wants to get our support in ’28 has to prioritize immigration reform, period," Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, D-Texas, who defeated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in South Texas, said last Wednesday at a news conference alongside fellow Texas Democrats pushing for immigration reform. But Fox News Digital polling showed 27% of Republican voters ranked immigration as their top issue, compared to just 3% of Democrats. Pulido flipped a redrawn, Republican-leaning South Texas district, ousting De La Cruz, who won her re-election in 2024 by 14. 2 points. He campaigned on affordability while tying Trump's immigration enforcement raids at worksites to workforce shortages that hurt the economy. REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital that voters who split their tickets between Trump and down-ballot Democrats in 2024 were responding this year to both affordability pressures and the president’s immigration crackdown. "He made a promise that he was going to bring prices down on day one. Liberation didn't happen, so people remembered that," Cuellar, whose district encompasses border town Laredo, told Fox News Digital. "Second thing is he said he was going to focus on criminals. He didn't stop there. He started going after construction workers." Democrats’ wins came as an estimated 14.5 million Latinos voted across the country in the 2026 midterms, according to UnidosUS. The group’s Texas state director, Eric Holguín, said Democratic support among Latino voters rivaled levels seen in 2008, when Barack Obama won the presidency. "Cost of living was the number one issue that we saw with Latino voters in Texas and across the country as well," Holguín told Fox News Digital, referring to polling conducted by UnidosUS. Pre-election polling conducted by Fox News Voter Poll, showed that for 45% of polled Hispanic voters, the economy was the most important issue facing the country, followed by the state of democracy for 26% of voters and then immigration at 15%. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE For Hispanics voting in Texas, polling followed a similar trend with the economy the number one issue for 45% of voters, the state of democracy for 25% of voters and immigration for 15%. "People right now, they see their pocketbooks, they see the bank accounts, they the grocery bills, they see they're electric bills, they see there gas bills and they're saying, 'Hey, a lot of promises were made to us in 2024 by President Trump, and he's had almost two years to deliver on those promises, and not only has he not delivered on those promise, he's made them worse with the war in Iran!,'" Holguín said. Trump said that the Iran war hurt Republicans in the midterms, as conflict in the Strait of Hormuz has destabilized oil supply chains, causing gas prices to soar. Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center, told Fox News Digital that voters were likely motivated by a rejection of Trump rather than enthusiasm for Democrats' policies. "It was driven by an anger that the president hasn't delivered on the promises that he made, particularly bringing down the cost of living and decreasing international tensions," Olsen said. "People see that inflation is higher than when he took office, and America is involved militarily in more places than they were under the Biden administration, and that's not what they thought they were getting." HISPANIC VOTERS ARE NATURAL CONSERVATIVES. REAGAN KNEW. GOP NEEDS TO PROVE IT AGAIN During a 60 Minutes interview, Trump said some of his deportations policies were "too tough"and that a deal with Democrats was "doable." Miguel Valenzuela, a business owner in Texas who joined American Families United for the Nov. 11 news conference, said he had spent years warning Republicans that their approach to immigration risked alienating Hispanic voters who otherwise shared some of the party’s values. "Hispanic values, family, faith, hardworking," Valenzuela, who does not identify as a Democrat, told Fox News Digital. "That sounds like a Republican, right? " Valenzuela said he had attended local Republican political events and urged the party to address immigration reform before pushing away an entire voting bloc. He argued that children of immigrants were reaching voting age and making their frustrations known at the ballot box. "Those kids have now became of age and they are voting. And since they are now voting, this is exactly what I had been warning about for years. And it happened last week," Valenzuela said. "They’re looking for major change in how our government’s run and how our government delivers for the people." Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Stop the political warfare against Elon Musk — our very survival may depend on him
articles.summary: For the sake of us all, we need to put hate aside and allow Elon Musk to figure out a way to place our species among the stars, before war, a virus, an asteroid or other cataclysmic event ends all life on Earth.
articles.body:
I get that many on the left are angry with Elon Musk. But as with the thousands of people who either celebrated or rationalized the assassination of Charlie Kirk last year — including people within the U.S. government and military — I cannot help but think that many of those who harbor an unhinged hatred for the visionary entrepreneur are literally hopeful for his demise as well.

According to an NPR-PBS News-Marist poll released in October 2025, 30 percent now believe we “may have to resort to violence to get the country back on track … up 11 points since April 2024.” When did killing a fellow human being simply because of differing political views become so acceptable to so many? Most especially if there is a chance that one of those lives threatened could save humanity , should the worst happen to our planet?

As someone who has long had one foot in the political world and the other in the space world, I am exceedingly happy that the contentious midterm election is now behind us, for a host of reasons. One reason is that despite the growing threats to investigate or even imprison Musk may free him up to devote much more of his brain power on how best to establish a large and permanent human presence in space .

The fact of the matter is that our species, at the direction of imperfect “leaders” living in bubbles of entitlement far from the working class of the world, has demonstrated an eagerness to wipe out wide swaths of humanity throughout history. The horrific war continuing to take place between Russia and Ukraine is just the latest example — a war that is littered with trip wires that could trigger a world-wide nuclear war.

If that’s not terrifying enough, we also have, as the world witnessed during the COVID pandemic, the very real possibility of an evil laboratory virus killing us all , or the rise of a new robotic overlord ?

With humanity at such a growing risk of extinction, don’t we want to hedge our bets and get some percentage of the human species permanently off the surface of Earth? Once upon a time, before the “Age of Trump” and hate before reason, Musk was really, really good at thinking of ways to get humankind permanently off the planet. For the sake of us all, we need to put hate aside and allow him to be that person again.

Like him or not, agree with him or not, Elon Musk does have a once-in-a-century mind. The kind of mind that when it is freed from poisonous partisan nonsense, has the exceptionally unique ability to focus on ways to propel a large cross-section of humanity into the cosmos.

To that critical quest, more than years ago, Musk gave a keynote speech at the 67th International Astronautical Congress, where he spoke of his dream to colonize Mars in an effort to protect humankind from “certain doom.”

He stressed : “Long term, it’s essential for preserving the light of consciousness. Eventually something will happen to Earth, hopefully not soon, either natural or man-made that would cause the end of civilization. The probable lifespan of civilization is much greater if we’re a multi-planet species.”

Musk is correct. We all must recognize that, and allow him the time and peace of mind to figure out a way to place our species among the stars, before war, a virus, an asteroid or other cataclysmic event ends all life on Earth.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Some Republicans say rising stars should sit out 2028 after midterm shellacking
articles.summary: Republicans are actively talking about the wisdom of GOP candidates skipping the 2028 presidential race and focusing on 2032, arguing the political atmosphere in two years will be too poisonous for their brand. The discussions come in the context of sweeping losses for the GOP in last week’s midterms, which have a number of Republicans…
articles.body:
Republicans are actively talking about the wisdom of GOP candidates skipping the 2028 presidential race and focusing on 2032, arguing the political atmosphere in two years will be too poisonous for their brand.

The discussions come in the context of sweeping losses for the GOP in last week’s midterms, which have a number of Republicans down in the dumps.

There are also real worries over President Trump, whose popularity has hit new lows but whose policies and political discussions will loom over Congress and the White House for the next two years.

That’s factoring into the decisions of some potential GOP presidential candidates.

“How can a candidate run in 2028 when they have to criticize the policies of a sitting president with a large amount of sway with the Republican base?” said one GOP operative who is close to a lawmaker weighing a future presidential bid. “It’s a suicide mission.”

“Unless there is a major shift in the direction of the country, where we end the war in Iran, reduce the cost of gas and groceries, and voters feel the White House is focused on their needs, I’m not sure any credible Republican candidate will run in 2028,” the operative said. “There is a strong feeling that the best chance a Republican has to win is in 2032 after these problems can be addressed and Trump is no longer a factor.”

Vice President Vance, who is the front-runner for the GOP nomination, has also been weighing whether to launch a bid for 2028. But since the thumping Republicans received in the midterms, Vance’s allies have wondered quietly if 2028 is the right time for Vance, still just 42 years old, to run for the White House.

“It may not be his time,” one former Trump aide said. “It’s going to be a tough time for any Republican to run for president in 2028 based on what happened last week.”

CNN reported Friday that Vance has given serious consideration to not running for president in 2028. While the outlet said the vice president has “yet to make up his mind,” those in his orbit said he’s been mulling the future of MAGA while also thinking about his family and his four young children. Vance wants to be a central part of the rebuilding effort for Republicans but also is unsure “whether he should be the one to lead it,” the report said.

Veteran GOP strategist Susan Del Percio said the uncertainty surrounding Vance’s political future and the reluctance of other Republicans to enter the race underscore the predicament facing the party.

“Trump will be the downfall of any 2028 nominee because they have to be 100 percent MAGA, and pass the MAGA loyalty test and no one can do that because you don’t know what the president will be for or against at any given moment,” Del Percio said. “We talk about how Trump’s numbers can’t get any worse. But they can. This is only the beginning.”

Trump has not endorsed Vance or any would-be candidate in the contest and allies say they don’t expect him to do so anytime soon.

Del Percio said that gives Vance an “out” not to run for president, if he chooses.

“The best scenario for JD Vance is to say he’s not running because he does not have the president’s endorsement,” she said. “If that’s the case, it allows him to bow out gracefully.”

On the other hand, Del Percio added, he could also use it as a way of securing the president’s endorsement and getting it early.

“It’s a way of softly forcing the president’s hand,” she continued. “If he does want to run, he has to get his endorsement and he needs to start running soon. He can’t leave room for speculation.”

It is, of course, early days after the GOP’s midterm disaster, and the political winds could change. After the 2024 elections, it was Democrats who were in the dumps, while Republicans imagined running Washington for some time.

Other Republican strategists involved in discussions about the upcoming election said the concerns about 2028 are real and that candidates are second-guessing the race. But they also said the GOP is hardly prepared to concede the next presidential election. Republicans will pour resources into the fight and mount aggressive campaigns, particularly in congressional races.

They’ll also be hoping that Democrats trip over themselves as they take command of the House and Senate. The GOP is hoping, and many Republicans say they are expecting, the Democrats in power to overreach, and potentially tarnish their own brand.

Yet at the same time, the presidential contest presents a different calculation. While Democrats are roaring to congressional power, the White House remains with Trump, leaving him with tremendous authority to run the country. That gives Democrats someone to run against for the next two years, too.

The mood right now in many GOP circles is dour on the 2028 cycle after the surprise wipeout in Texas, and Senate defeats in states such as Mississippi and South Carolina.

“Everybody is still in the fog of defeat but no one is confident that 2028 is going to be appreciably better,” said one national Republican consultant who worked on midterm races. “We’re gonna play, we’re gonna spend a ton of money, and we’re going to do better than we did because it was so bad this time.

“But as far as flipping these institutions and winning the White House, no one thinks that’s in the cards for 2028,” the consultant said.

One former Trump campaign aide disagreed with that assessment, saying that Republicans have time to figure it out in the coming months.

“I know RNC members are specifically looking at how to rebound and win in 2028, which is why Jon Gruters is getting so much pushback in his effort to try to run for chair again and will likely lose,” the former aide said, referring to the chair of the Republican National Committee. “Giving up on 2028 when the Democratic Congress hasn’t even been sworn in strikes me as not only premature, but has to come from the same loser consultants who spent hundreds of millions of dollars to have the worst election in 50 years.”

Republicans acknowledge being worn down after the disastrous cycle.

There’s “massive donor fatigue” from the midterms, the GOP consultant said. Republicans also say they are also bracing for two more years of the Trump presidency, and some fear an administration that now includes Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff could harm the GOP brand.

“Donald Trump is not going to reinvent himself,” said one former Trump aide. “Does anyone think he’s going to change course? Does anyone think he’s going to be more conciliatory? He is doubling down with Stephen Miller.

“The general consensus is that we’re f‑‑‑ed until Donald Trump leaves office,” the former Trump aide said.

As far as 2028 goes, the former aide said, “someone gets to be the sacrificial lamb, that’s how a lot of people are looking at it. Some candidates will do it to develop a national donor network, get their name out there and come back with a much better set of cards in 2032.

“The only shot we have right now is if Democrats do a bunch of cooky s‑‑‑ and nominate a super progressive,” the former Trump aide said. “That’s the dream scenario for 2028.”

articles.title: White House lawyer's hardball warning to Dems has legal experts on both sides questioning one key threat
articles.summary: William Scharf's letter warns Democrats that abusive subpoenas could cross into criminality, but Rep. Robert Garcia says Trump has something to hide.
articles.body: Counsel to the president William Scharf sent a letter to House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform ranking member California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia Nov. 9, warning Democrats against running afoul of their allotted powers pertaining to investigations and subpoenas. The letter put Democratic lawmakers on notice to remind them of the "foundational limits that the Constitution imposes on congressional investigations and subpoenas" and suggesting that their actions could cross the line of criminal misconduct. Garcia, who is poised to chair the committee next year when Democrats gain the House majority, responded to the letter suggesting that the president has "something to hide." Legal experts from across the political spectrum who spoke to Fox News Digital suggested that, while the White House is within its rights to challenge individual subpoenas, it faces significant obstacles if it decides to seek criminal indictments related to Garcia's oversight activities. "In short, the administration can assert privileges, negotiate over requests and challenge particular subpoenas through the appropriate legal process, but criminal prosecutions are, to mix metaphors, a very different animal that face a higher bar," Ilya Shapiro, director of constitutional studies at the right-of-center Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital. AG BLANCHE CLASHES WITH ANCHOR ASKING WHETHER IT'S HIS 'JOB' TO DEFEND THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION Congressional investigations also enjoy protections under the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which the Supreme Court has held shields lawmakers from judicial interference when their investigative activities fall within the legitimate legislative sphere. Shapiro explained that Democrats who are "promising indiscriminate subpoenas are inviting challenges to their demands" as congressional committees "must act within their jurisdiction, respect witnesses’ constitutional rights and connect investigations to a legitimate legislative purpose." Garcia, however, maintains that his calls for investigation are totally consistent with his constitutional authority as a lawmaker. "Let’s be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said in his statement. "The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse. The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers," Garcia stated. Scharf sent the letter a week after Democrats issued statements and social media posts on calling for subpoenas and impeachment trials for Trump administration officials after Republicans suffered a major loss during the 2026 midterms. At the time, some pointed out that Republicans used similar language to call for investigations into Democratic officials. Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom and a constitutional law expert, told Fox News Digital that Scharf is correct in his assertion that Garcia's investigations cannot be motivated by simple spite, but suggested that the White House may run into problems if they try to get criminal charges to stick. "Scharf is correct in his citation of Watkins v. U.S. that the Supreme Court has held that congressional investigations not connected to a legitimate legislative purpose and whose only intent is harassment and trying to seize personal, private information are unconstitutional and beyond the power of Congress," von Spakovsky wrote in an email. "Problem is that I am not sure what criminal statutes, if any, could be applied. There are statutes over harassment of federal officials, 18 U.S.C. 111, 115, but those require physical threats. What the Watkins precedent holds is that the courts cannot enforce subpoenas issued by Congress that are part of an improper, unconstitutional investigation." TOP DEM ON COMMITTEE FIRES BACK AFTER WHITE HOUSE COUNSEL WARNS AGAINST OVERREACH AMID INVESTIGATION THREATS "No statute makes oversight a crime, and Scharf’s letter doesn't say one does. Its point is that a committee's process doesn't shield conduct that would be a crime for anyone else. Conspiring to intimidate federal officers out of doing their jobs falls under 18 U.S.C. 372," Will Chamberlain, senior counsel at the right-of-center Article III Project, told Fox News Digital. "Congress's oversight authority is broad but not unlimited. There is no congressional power to expose for the sake of exposure and any investigation requires a valid legislative purpose. Congressional investigative activity conducted in an official capacity wouldn't be prosecutable." He added that, what could be prosecutable, would be a separate conspiracy to intimidate federal officials "evidenced by threats, press releases, things of that nature." Molly Nixon, a senior fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute, had broadly similar thoughts. "White House Counsel is correct that courts have required congressional investigations to serve a legitimate legislative purpose, though the constitutional boundaries of that requirement are not as clear as Scharf asserts. I don’t think the letter is on solid ground when it makes the leap to suggesting potential criminality," she told Fox News Digital. DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS "We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government. Recent public statements underscore these concerns. You and your congressional colleagues have asserted that they will issue subpoenas to harass, threaten, and deter dedicated members of the Administration from further service," wrote Scharf. "Compulsory process is a power Congress has for oversight functions, and only for oversight functions. Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end," the letter continued. "Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality," the letter continued. "And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation." Those further investigations, however, are unlikely to result in criminal charges, according Devon Ombres, senior director for courts and legal policy at the left-of-center Center for American Progress. "You know, I don't think that there is any reasonable basis for the administration to argue that Congress cannot undertake its constitutional obligations of conducting oversight, and I can't imagine that there's any type of criminal statute that would apply in this context," he said in a phone call. "That's not to say that this DOJ won't try and shoehorn something in, as they've already done, but I don't think that Scharf has a legal leg to stand on." While criminal charges would face significant legal obstacles, Ombres says he fully expects the Trump administration to try blocking the subpoenas through lawsuits. articles.title: Fetterman: Naming Van Hollen majority leader ‘would be troubling’
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) hinted that he could leave the Democratic Party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is elected as the Senate Majority Leader. “Yeah, absolutely, it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti … hostile to Israel,” Fetterman said when…
articles.body:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) hinted that he could leave the Democratic Party if Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is elected as the Senate Majority Leader.

“Yeah, absolutely, it would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen that has really made his name being very anti … hostile to Israel,” Fetterman said when asked if there is a “red line” for him to walk away from the party, in a Fox News interview .

Fetterman’s remarks come after Van Hollen said Thursday that he would challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the role of the majority leader.

“In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption,” Van Hollen wrote in a post on social platform X . “To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call.”

Fetterman has previously warned that if the Democratic party becomes “the anti-Israel party,” he would leave.

In his recent Fox interview, Fetterman said, “If you are going to be angry or hostile towards any countries in the region, why not make that, you know, Iran, or Hezbollah or Hamas as well too?.”

Shortly after the midterm elections, where Democrats swept up the country in a “blue wave,” Schumer said that he expects to have the votes to be elected as the majority leader.

Several Democrats have said they would not back Schumer. This includes Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), as well as incoming senators Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.), Annie Andrews (D-S.C.), Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Troy Jackson (D-Maine).

The leadership bids come after the Democrats secured a sweeping victory in the midterm elections last week, taking control of both chambers of Congress. The party currently holds 55 Senate seats, after Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the state’s competitive Senate race.

The only state that has not called its Senate race is Alaska, where Democrat Mary Peltola is challenging Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

articles.title: The MAGA-lomaniacs who could drag America into the abyss
articles.summary: Recent midterm elections resulted in a significant rebuke of the Trump administration, prompting criticism of unfulfilled campaign promises from both former allies like Tucker Carlson and Vice President JD Vance.
articles.body:
The midterms hit the Republican Party like a gut punch. Voters delivered a clear, undeniable rebuke to the Trump administration, turning the entire election into a referendum on unfulfilled pledges and persistent pandemonium.

The Trump brand, once viewed by millions with something approaching religious reverence, now looks toxic to swing voters, suburban parents, independents across the nation, and anyone with a functioning pair of eyes. Those who still believe this administration will deliver on its foundational promises need to sit down and do some serious soul-searching.

In other words, they need to take a page from Tucker Carlson’s playbook. The reformed cable news host and passionate nicotine pouch peddler recently released a fifteen-minute video systematically detailing every promise the administration has broken since President Trump was reelected. Carlson paid special attention to the president’s vow to avoid starting new foreign wars.

He also dragged out the old campaign claim that the Russia-Ukraine conflict would end within 24 hours of taking office. That particular promise dissolved into thin air the second it met the reality of global diplomacy and a man named Vladimir Putin. When your most enthusiastic cheerleaders put down the pom-poms and start creating video montages of your most egregious lies and failures, you have to ask serious questions.

Inside the West Wing, instead of asking questions, Trump is doubling down. His second term has been a genuine mess, farcical even, but it has now descended into something resembling a soap opera written by toddlers. So desperate to fill the press secretary role, the president took to social media, practically begging UFC head Dana White to consider swapping the business of professional combat for the realm of political combat. Trump insists he was merely joking , but one could be forgiven for thinking that a man with a questionable relationship to truth-telling was not telling the truth.

Things are so bad that one should expect Kid Rock to get a call soon, asking whether he has any interest in replacing impeachment-prone Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Following the abrupt departure of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the search for her replacement exposed just how radioactive the current administration has become. Stephen Miller , the ultimate bureaucratic Bond villain, quickly filled the slot.

Critics routinely describe Miller as a megalomaniac , but he can at least be described as a MAGA-lomaniac whose position of power represents a genuine threat to functional governance. He is not only ambitious but also has an absolute immunity to real-world facts. When high-level policy stems entirely from an individual’s inflated sense of destiny and genuine contempt for the opposition, federal agencies stop solving real problems and start serving as instruments to validate a very specific agenda.

Doubting the administration’s trajectory is no longer a habit restricted to opposition politicians. Vice President JD Vance aired his own sharp critique shortly after the midterm vote tallies were finalized. In a candid post-election piece, Vance admitted that voters had soundly rejected the party’s current direction. He singled out the growing conflict with Iran as the single biggest factor that drove voters away and crippled conservative turnout. When the sitting vice president explicitly blames his own administration’s foreign policy for an electoral disaster, any illusion of internal harmony disappears.

Looking forward to the 2028 presidential contest, the intersection of MAGA-lomania and election denial poses a severe threat. If current economic and political trends hold, the Democratic Party has a clear path to securing the presidency in two years. Voters have clearly shown their disdain for Trump and his insufferable loyalists.

Democrats are feeling emboldened, and it’s easy to see why. But even if they are victorious in 2028, they should know that winning an election in modern-day America is no longer synonymous with a smooth, peaceful transfer of executive power. An administration controlled by figures who view their authority as absolute may not accept electoral defeat, no matter how resounding the thumping may be.

To a vindictive, borderline delusional administration, losing a democratic vote is less a sign of public dissatisfaction than an impossible event that must be overturned. The next presidential election won’t be only about who gets the most votes in key states, but also about whether American governing institutions can survive a disgraced and defeated incumbent who would rather wreck the political house than make way for the next occupant.

The midterm outcome showed that voters eventually reach a saturation point with endless drama and countless betrayals. Rhetoric can carry a political movement through an election cycle, but it can’t sustain an administration when basic promises go unkept year after year. Continuing to believe in a political brand that routinely breaks its word requires ignoring every hard fact that has emerged over the past few years.

The recent election proved that a decisive majority of the country has finally stopped pretending not to see what is happening right in front of them. The question is whether MAGA is truly dead, or preparing to turn its final act into a full-scale scorched-earth campaign. If I were a betting man, I would put my money on the latter.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Justice Alito warns America must preserve 3 core principles regardless of country’s ‘atmosphere’
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito outlined three principles he says Americans must always prioritize amid the 2026 midterms and the Iran War.
articles.body: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito recently laid out three principles Americans must cling to to ensure the integrity of the republic: freedom of speech, religious liberty and racial equality. "I'm not saying we're entering the dark age, but these are things that we have to preserve no matter what the atmosphere is in the country or the world at the time," Alito said during a fireside chat with Mollie Hemingway, editor-in-chief at the Federalist, which followed the Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner at the 2026 National Lawyer's Convention in Washington D.C. The remarks come on the heels of the blue tsunami of the 2026 midterms, with Republicans losing 42 House seats and eight Senate seats, with the Alaska U.S. Senate race still uncalled. Democrats are set to take control of Congress with eight lawmakers backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Both incoming and returning members have pressed for investigations and subpoenas targeting President Donald Trump and his administration. DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN Alito's remarks also come amid the ongoing Iran war, which has destabilized oil supply chains across the globe, causing the price of goods and gas to jump. The 76-year-old jurist said preserving freedom of speech is paramount, warning that "you cannot have Democratic self-fulfillment if you cannot have robust free speech." "Even speech that is hurtful to some of the people who hear what is being said," Alito said. He also stressed the importance of freedom of religion, even as the Supreme Court is set to rule on at least two major cases this term centered on religious freedom: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy and Grand v. City of University Heights. SUPREME COURT OFFERS SUPPORT FOR CATHOLIC PRESCHOOLS CHALLENGING STATE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS "I think that we have placed religious liberty on a sounder footing than it was on 20, 25 years ago," Alito said. "Religious liberty is central to human dignity, and in a society that is as religiously diverse as this country, we've got people who adhere to practically every religion that exists in the world," Alito continued. "We are not going to be able to get along, I think, amicably, productively, if we don't respect everybody's right to follow whatever religion they want, or for people of faith, they're also free to do that." "That's essential," Alito said. He rounded off his trifecta by saying that America must maintain racial equality, declaring it "essential for our pluralistic society." FEDERAL JUDGE TOSSES TRUMP ADMIN HARVARD ADMISSIONS LAWSUIT, LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO FUTURE CHALLENGE "That is the principle that Dr. Martin Luther King famously articulated in his speech at the Lincoln Memorial, where he said he looked forward to the day when children would be judged by the content of their character and not by the color of their skin," Alito said. "If we don't hold to that principle, then I think the society is going to start to come apart," Alito said. The Supreme Court agreed in October to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education this term, a challenge brought by parents of Asian American students alleging that a Maryland school district’s admissions policies unlawfully discriminate despite appearing race-neutral. Alito mentioned the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, which ended affirmative action in college admissions, as among the most consequential rulings from the Supreme Court in the past few decades. TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME' Alito's discussion comes as questions swirl about his possible plans to retire. In a Bloomberg article published after the midterms, Alito said that the Democrats' sweep did not change his plans to stay on the Supreme Court. Alito, nominated by President George W. Bush, has served on the bench since 2006. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "With those, with those 20 years, I jumped to 42nd in the the list of all-time service by Supreme Court justices," Alito said.

articles.title: Former top FAA official warns of 48-hour recovery after aging tech 'overwhelmed' ahead of ground stop
articles.summary: Pilots, a former FAA official and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy explain the nationwide ground stop, detailing the telecom overload, 48-hour recovery and funding push.
articles.body: A former top FAA official who helped shut down New York airspace on 9/11 urged Congress to fund an overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system after equipment problems led to a nationwide ground stop. Speaking on "Fox & Friends Weekend" on Saturday, former FAA air traffic senior executive Mike McCormick said Friday's outage highlighted the challenge of updating the agency's aging technology. "It is always a challenge to do any modernization, update or technical refresh into the FAA's air traffic control system. It's similar to if you're going to change a tire on a car while it's still moving down the road," McCormick said while discussing the outage. "The newer technology overwhelmed the pre-existing technology, and it led to the overload of the switching and associated software in the telecommunications system," he added. "And that led to communication problems, and then eventually the nationwide shutdown." THOUSANDS OF FLIGHTS CANCELED AFTER LONGEST NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP IN 25 YEARS ROCKS US AIRPORTS McCormick said he supports funding initiatives aimed at upgrading the nation's air traffic control system, emphasizing that the technology must meet both current and future demands. NBA AND NHL TEAMS BATTLE DELAYS AS NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS WEEKEND SPORTS TRAVEL Although flights have resumed, McCormick warned that it could take days for air travel to return to normal. "This will take several days in order to be able to get all of the aircraft, all the passengers, all the baggage, all of the flight crews, all where they need to be positioned to get the system up and running from early morning through the evening," he said. "So I would predict at least 48 hours in order to restore this completely." At a Saturday news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the outage began when a contractor performing routine maintenance at a remote FAA facility attempted to replace outdated copper lines with fiber-optic cables. Duffy said a replacement router installed during the work flooded the agency's telecommunications network, triggering radar and radio instability. Duffy and Bedford said investigators found no evidence of a cyberattack. FAA BREAKS CONTROLLER HIRING RECORD AFTER CHIEF WARNED SYSTEM WAS 'CHRONICALLY UNDERSTAFFED' "Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money, and they provide really poor service to us. Full stop," Duffy said, adding that he plans to submit a detailed funding request to Congress covering telecommunications upgrades and improvements to aging runways and control towers. "This was an FAA system that didn't meet the moment, our contractor didn't meet the moment or the equipment didn't meet the moment, and caused the outages," Duffy said. WHEN AIRLINE PILOTS SAY THERE ARE SAFETY ISSUES, WE NEED POLICYMAKERS TO LISTEN AND ACT Despite the widespread disruptions, aviation experts said the decision to halt flights demonstrated the safety measures built into the nation's air traffic system. Josh Schirard, a commercial pilot and head of law enforcement at Byrna Technologies, said the incident showed that the aviation system prioritizes passenger safety over convenience. He praised pilots, air traffic controllers and flight crews for safely bringing aircraft to the ground. "The big takeaway from what we saw over the last 24 hours really is for the American traveler, how safe our air system really is, and yesterday was a great illustration of that," Schirard said. "Through the safety of the infrastructure that does exist – through the pilots, the crew, the controllers, through the airplanes themselves and really the redundancy of protocols and practices that are in place – that all combined is what allowed us to take 3,500 planes in a matter of hours and over a million travelers and get them on the ground safely," he said. Scott Pattillo, a retired United Airlines pilot, said his initial reaction to a nationwide ground stop would have been disbelief if he had been flying at the time. "Well, first thing I think is, 'Holy crap, is this real? Is this really happening on a Friday the 13th?' And second thing, it harps back to 9/11, and we all remember what that was like, especially if we were working and flying during that time," he said. "So the first thing, as a pilot, is I'm not [going to] panic." Pattillo explained that, based on his understanding, the outage disrupted radar data and radio communications for high-altitude air traffic controllers. Airport towers and controllers handling arriving aircraft, however, relied on separate technology that was not affected by the same outage. Pattillo said that distinction allowed pilots already in the air to continue along their assigned routes and safely reach their destinations. "As a pilot, you have to remain predictable," Pattillo said. "And you're trained under certain scenarios what to do. And the best thing to do is continue on that path." Pattillo also defended the decision to ground flights nationwide, calling it "absolutely" the right move. articles.body:
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) called on Howard Lutnick, President Trump’s Commerce secretary, to step down over reports the cabinet member shielded Nvidia from federal oversight — accusations which emerged after the tech giant’s CEO resigned this week.

Jensen Huang stepped down from Nvidia’s chief role Thursday after claims came to light of his reported infidelity — with one of these affairs apparently involving an alleged Chinese spy. The event sparked national security concerns and raised questions about what Trump officials, including Lutnick, knew about the possible espionage.

Blumenthal said in a Friday social media post , “Lutnick must go,” in response to an opinion article in Fortune accusing the secretary of blocking oversight of the AI giant — despite calls from within Trump’s cabinet to intervene.

“His malign self-enriching malfeasance shows the costs of corruption—putting personal profit above public interest,” the senator wrote. “Making powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security & economic competitiveness.”

Ahead of Huang’s resignation, Axios reported last week that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over the Commerce Department’s decision not to add Nvidia customer Megaspeed to a list of companies that pose national security concerns.

The alleged Chinese spy with whom Jensen admitted to having an affair, Alice Huang, was a Megaspeed employee.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to use their congressional oversight powers to investigate members of the Trump administration for alleged infractions when they gain control of the legislature next year.

On Thursday, the top Democrats on the House’s and Senate’s trade committees requested Commerce Department officials — including Lutnick — preserve their records on Trump’s decision last year to green light Nvidia’s sale of its powerful H200 chips to China.

In a follow-up social media post Friday afternoon, Blumenthal emphasized that “corruption has costs.”

“China’s access to this key AI resource endangers not only our military defense—but also economic growth, jobs & more,” he said. “Whether by resignation or firing, his departure is imperative, & well deserved.”

The Hill has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.
